rv.q: ‘Black Superhero’ is messy and over-ambitious, but it’s empathetic and perceptive.
Black Superhero, the debut play from Olivier award-nominated actor and activist Danny Lee Wynter, feels simultaneously flawed, audacious, and inventive.
Daniel Evans’s fierce production cannot disguise the fact that Wynter edges around this pertinently current issue without adding much incisive clarity to the debate.
But by the end, you leave feeling you have been eavesdropping on an overlong therapy session.

Some theatrical works defy description and so it is with BLACK SUPERHERO currently playing at the The Theatre. No stranger to controversy, the venue has long ceased apologising for its part in bringing challenging avant garde work to the fore. It justifiably revels in its reputation and by presenting new work as strong as this, it is right to do so.

Even when it fires in too many directions at once — which is much of the time — BLACK SUPERHERO courses with a singular energy and fervour that more than compensate for the occasionally pro forma language.
BLACK SUPERHERO is a consistently entertaining if scattered reflection on friendship, love, family and queer identities that is often very funny but sometimes loses its central thread.
Despite its flaws, Daniel Evans' crisp direction keeps the tone buoyant balancing the comedic elements with serious intrigue.
Yet it remains a frustrating evening, full of potential, but lacking in superpower.
Despite this interesting material about identity and activism, Black Superhero is clumsy in its storytelling, and the good jokes don’t make up for the uncertain tone of the writing.
Perhaps then we should just take the initials and categorise the show as a heady dose of BS.

cn.t: Critics are divided on Wynter's ambitious debut exploring Black queer identity through a superhero lens. Some praise its audacity and entertainment value, while others find it scattered, overwrought, and struggling to cohere its many themes.
